title: Simplification
summary: BODMAS, identity-based fractions, surds and indices, square/cube roots and approximation. These are the fastest marks in Tier 1 — usually 1–2 questions per shift — and the same skills (identities, surd handling) power the algebra questions.

subtopics.title: BODMAS, 'of', brackets & vinculum
subtopics.concept: VBODMAS fixes the order: vinculum bar first, then brackets innermost first, then 'of', then division and multiplication left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right. The one trap that costs marks is 'of', which multiplies before any division sign.

formulas.name: 'Of' before division
formulas.tex: a \div b \text{ of } c = a \div (b \times c)

formulas.name: Division and multiplication left to right

tricks.title: Bracket every 'of'
tricks.body: Rewrite each 'of' as a bracketed product before doing any division. The bracket makes the grouping visible and kills the trap.

tricks.title: Continued fractions from the bottom
tricks.body: Simplify the deepest fraction first, invert it, add the next layer, and repeat upward.

tricks.title: Digit-sum check
tricks.body: Casting out nines: digit sums must match on both sides of the equals sign. It kills wrong options without computing the product.

steps: Product must be a multiple of 9. $699678 \to 45 \to 9$. So it can.

mistakes.wrong: Computing a divided by b times c as a divided by (b times c).
mistakes.right: Division and multiplication share a rank: work left to right.

mistakes.wrong: Treating 'of' like an ordinary multiplication done after division.
mistakes.right: 'Of' groups its two numbers into a product before any division acts.

mistakes.wrong: Opening a square bracket before the round bracket inside it.
mistakes.right: Clear the innermost bracket first; each layer becomes one number.

mistakes.wrong: Keeping the inner signs when a minus precedes a bracket.
mistakes.right: A minus before a bracket flips every sign inside it.

mistakes.wrong: Clearing a vinculum bar after the brackets.
mistakes.right: The bar is the V in VBODMAS; it goes first.

subtopics.notes:
A long expression with several operations is worked in one fixed order, called VBODMAS: Vinculum, Brackets, Of, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction. The whole method lives in one example: $64 \div 4 \text{ of } 2$ is $64 \div 8 = 8$, while $64 \div 4 \times 2$ is $16 \times 2 = 32$.

### The order, step by step
1. V for vinculum: a bar over an expression, like $\overline{9 - 7}$, is cleared first.
2. B for brackets: innermost first, $( )$ then $\{ \}$ then $[ ]$.
3. O for of: 'of' means multiply, but it happens before $\div$ and $\times$.
4. D and M: division and multiplication, strictly left to right.
5. A and S: addition and subtraction, again left to right.

> **Rule:** 'Of' outranks the division sign. Convert every 'of' into a bracketed product before touching any $\div$.

### Where 'of' goes wrong
$64 \div 4 \text{ of } 2$ means $64 \div (4 \times 2) = 8$, not $(64 \div 4) \times 2 = 32$. The examiner builds both versions into the options. The same trap appears with fractions: $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of $48 \div 2$ is $\left(\dfrac{3}{4} \times 48\right) \div 2 = 18$.

> **Watch:** Percentages work the same way: $40\%$ of $250$ is a product $\dfrac{40}{100} \times 250$, done before any division outside it.

### Clearing brackets
Start with the innermost bracket and move outward, one layer at a time. A minus sign in front of a bracket flips every sign inside: $25 - (10 - 6) = 25 - 10 + 6 = 21$. Never open all layers in one go; each layer must become a single number first.

### Division and multiplication share a rank
When only $\div$ and $\times$ appear, walk left to right: $60 \div 5 \times 3 = 12 \times 3 = 36$. Doing $60 \div 15 = 4$ instead is the standard slip, and 4 is always among the options.

### Continued fractions
A fraction inside a fraction is simplified from the bottom up. For $1 + \dfrac{1}{1 + \dfrac{1}{2}}$: the bottom gives $1 + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}$, then $\dfrac{1}{3/2} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, then $1 + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{5}{3}$. Keep fractions as fractions; decimals half way through breed errors.

> **Tip:** Invert the bottom result and add one layer up, every time. Never clear the stack top-down.

### Two fast checks
Digit-sum check: replace each number by its digit sum and repeat the operation; the digit sum of your answer must match. $48 + 36 = 84$: digit sums $3 + 9 \to 12 \to 3$, and $84 \to 12 \to 3$. Last-digit check: for products and sums, work only with last digits. $7 \times 8 + 6 = 62$, and last digits $6 + 6 \to 2$ agree.

patterns.name: 'Of' before division and multiplication
patterns.howToSpot: The expression mixes division, multiplication and 'of' (or '% of'), often with a question mark in place of one number.
patterns.formula: a \div b \text{ of } c = a \div (b \times c)
steps: Replace every 'of' by a bracketed product.
Do division and multiplication left to right.
Finish with addition and subtraction left to right.
For a missing value, simplify the rest and solve the small equation.
patterns.why: 'Of' is a multiplication that the convention ranks above the division sign.

patterns.name: Vinculum and three-layer brackets
patterns.howToSpot: An expression carries a bar over some digits and nested round, curly and square brackets.
steps: Then the round bracket, then the curly, then the square.
Flip every sign inside a bracket that follows a minus.
patterns.why: Each layer must collapse to a single number before the layer outside it can act.

patterns.name: Continued (nested) fractions
patterns.howToSpot: Fractions stack inside fractions, written as small stacked numbers on the paper.
steps: Start at the deepest fraction and make it a single fraction.
Invert it and add the next layer up.
Repeat to the top; keep exact fractions, not decimals.
patterns.why: Each fraction line is a division, and the deepest division must happen first.

patterns.name: Long division-multiplication chains
patterns.howToSpot: A plain chain like division, times, plus, times, minus with no 'of' and no brackets.
patterns.formula: \div \text{ and } \times \text{ share a level: go left to right}
steps: Walk the expression once, left to right, doing only division and multiplication.
Collect the additions and subtractions for a second pass.
patterns.why: Division and multiplication have equal rank, so the leftmost one acts first.

patterns.name: Full mixed expression with fractions and percent
patterns.howToSpot: A longer expression mixes 'of', a fraction term and a percentage term.
steps: Turn 'of' terms into products and percentages into fractions over 100.
Combine the terms; the fraction parts usually divide neatly.
patterns.why: Term-by-term simplification avoids one unreadable giant line.

'Of' beats $\div$ and $\times$; bracket the 'of' product first.
Minus before a bracket flips every sign inside.
Continued fractions: simplify bottom-up, keeping fractions.
Check answers with digit sums and last digits.

subtopics.title: Algebraic identities in numerical simplification
subtopics.concept: Many simplification questions are algebra identities with numbers pasted in. Name $a$ and $b$, match the signs, and the giant cubes cancel into a one-line answer like $a + b$ or $a - b$.

tricks.title: Pattern-match the fraction
tricks.body: Cubes on top and three terms with a middle product below mean a sum or difference of cubes. The fraction is just a plus or minus of the bases.

tricks.title: Zero-sum check before cubing
tricks.body: Add the three bases. If they sum to zero, the cubes sum to three times their product, signs included.

tricks.title: Products around a round number
tricks.body: Write the pair as centre minus gap and centre plus gap. The product is centre squared minus gap squared.

mistakes.wrong: Pairing a sum-of-cubes top with a plus middle term below.
mistakes.right: The middle sign below is opposite to the sign on top.

mistakes.wrong: Cubing the decimals in an identity fraction.
mistakes.right: Name a and b, cancel the factor, subtract or add the bases.

mistakes.wrong: Writing $(a+b)^3 = a^3 + b^3$.
mistakes.right: The cube of a sum carries the extra term $3ab(a+b)$.

mistakes.wrong: Using $k^2 + 2$ when $x + 1/x = k$ is given.
mistakes.right: Plus version subtracts 2; minus version adds 2.

mistakes.wrong: Applying the zero-sum rule without adding the bases.
mistakes.right: Check $a + b + c = 0$ first; otherwise cube honestly.

subtopics.notes:
A cube of $9.3$ looks like hard work until you notice the shape underneath. $\dfrac{9.3^3 - 3.3^3}{9.3^2 + 9.3 \times 3.3 + 3.3^2}$ collapses to $9.3 - 3.3 = 6$ because the denominator is exactly the second factor of $a^3 - b^3$. That is the whole game: spot the identity, name $a$ and $b$, substitute at the end.

### The identities that do the work
| Identity | Reads as |
|---|---|
| $a^3 + b^3 = (a+b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)$ | sum of cubes |
| $a^3 - b^3 = (a-b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)$ | difference of cubes |
| $a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b)$ | difference of squares |
| $(a+b)^2 + (a-b)^2 = 2(a^2+b^2)$ | squares combine |
| $(a+b)^2 - (a-b)^2 = 4ab$ | squares subtract |

> **Rule:** In an identity fraction, the sign in the denominator is opposite to the sign on top. Minus below pairs with plus above.

### Identity fractions
Read the denominator first, because it tells you what cancels. If the top is a difference of cubes and the bottom has a plus middle term, the whole fraction is $a - b$. Check $\dfrac{12.4^3 - 2.4^3}{12.4^2 + 12.4 \times 2.4 + 2.4^2}$: the bottom is the plus version, so the value is $12.4 - 2.4 = 10$. Never cube the decimals.

### Squares that sit near each other
$115^2 - 85^2 = (115 - 85)(115 + 85) = 30 \times 200 = 6000$. Whenever two squares sit close together, factor instead of squaring. The same identity multiplies numbers around a round value: $997 \times 1003 = 1000^2 - 3^2 = 999991$.

> **Tip:** Look for a shared centre. Write the pair as centre minus gap and centre plus gap, then use centre squared minus gap squared.

### The x plus one over x ladder
If $x + \dfrac{1}{x} = k$, then $x^2 + \dfrac{1}{x^2} = k^2 - 2$, and $x^3 + \dfrac{1}{x^3} = k^3 - 3k$. With the minus version the twos flip: if $x - \dfrac{1}{x} = k$, then $x^2 + \dfrac{1}{x^2} = k^2 + 2$. So $x + \dfrac{1}{x} = 4$ gives $16 - 2 = 14$ for the square, and $x + \dfrac{1}{x} = 6$ gives $36 - 2 = 34$.

### Cubes from a sum and a product
Given $a+b$ and $ab$, never hunt for $a$ and $b$. Use $a^2 + b^2 = (a+b)^2 - 2ab$ and $a^3 + b^3 = (a+b)^3 - 3ab(a+b)$. With $a+b = 7$ and $ab = 12$: $a^3 + b^3 = 343 - 252 = 91$, which is $3^3 + 4^3$.

### Zero-sum cubes
If $a + b + c = 0$, then $a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc$. Test the bases before cubing anything: $17 - 10 - 7 = 0$, so $17^3 + (-10)^3 + (-7)^3 = 3 \times 17 \times 10 \times 7 = 3570$. Two negative bases multiply to a positive here, so the sign needs one careful look.

> **Watch:** Add the three bases first. If they do not sum to zero, this shortcut does not apply and the numbers must be cubed honestly.

### A safe attacking order
1. Read the denominator of any fraction; it names the identity.
2. Match the middle sign to choose the plus or minus version.
3. Keep $a$ and $b$ symbolic until the expression is factored.
4. Substitute the numbers in the last line only.

patterns.name: Identity fraction: cubes over the quadratic factor
patterns.howToSpot: A fraction with cubed decimals on top and three terms with a middle product below.
steps: Read the sign of the middle term in the denominator.
Pick the matching identity: minus below pairs with plus above.
Add or subtract the two bases; that is the answer.
patterns.why: The denominator is literally the second factor of the numerator's factorisation.

steps: Bottom is the plus version, so the fraction equals $a - b$.

patterns.name: Squares near each other; round-about products
patterns.howToSpot: Two squares of close numbers, or a product of two numbers placed symmetrically around a round value.
steps: Find the centre: the average of the two numbers.
Find the gap: the distance from the centre to either number.
Multiply the sum by the difference, or use centre squared minus gap squared.
patterns.why: Factoring avoids squaring three-digit numbers by hand.

patterns.name: The x plus one over x ladder
patterns.howToSpot: A given value of $x + \frac{1}{x}$ or $x - \frac{1}{x}$, and a target square, cube or fourth power.
steps: Square the given relation; the cross term is $\pm 2$.
Plus version subtracts 2, minus version adds 2.
For cubes use $k^3 \mp 3k$; for fourth powers, square the square result and subtract 2.
patterns.why: Squaring $x \pm \frac{1}{x}$ produces the cross term $2$ or $-2$ beside the wanted square-sum.

patterns.name: Given a + b and ab
patterns.howToSpot: The pair sum and product are given; the target is a square-sum, cube-sum or a similar symmetric value.
steps: Write the target using only $(a+b)$ and $ab$.
If the numbers themselves are wanted, spot the small integer pair.
patterns.why: Every symmetric expression in two letters is a function of their sum and product.

patterns.name: Zero-sum cubes
patterns.howToSpot: Three cubes, often with negative or fractional bases, whose bases add to zero.
steps: Add the three bases and confirm the sum is zero.
Triple the product, watching the signs.
patterns.why: The identity for $a^3+b^3+c^3 - 3abc$ carries the factor $(a+b+c)$, which is zero here.

revision: $\dfrac{a^3 \pm b^3}{a^2 \mp ab + b^2} = a \pm b$.
$a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b)$ for near squares and round-about products.
$x + \dfrac{1}{x} = k$: square gives $k^2 - 2$, cube gives $k^3 - 3k$.
$a^3 + b^3 = (a+b)^3 - 3ab(a+b)$ from a sum and a product.
$a + b + c = 0$ gives $a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc$.
Substitute numbers only in the last line.

subtopics.title: Surds & indices
subtopics.concept: Indices rewrite every number as a power of one prime, then the exponents do the work. Surds rationalise through the conjugate, split via $x + y = a$ and $xy = b$, and compare after raising to a common root order.

tricks.title: Common base, then equate powers
tricks.body: Write both sides as powers of the same prime. The equation becomes a linear equation in the exponent.

tricks.title: Split a + 2 root b
tricks.body: Force the middle term into the 2 root b shape, then find two numbers with the given sum and product.

tricks.title: Reciprocal by the a squared minus b check
tricks.body: For x = a + sqrt(b), test a squared minus b. If it equals 1, the reciprocal is a minus sqrt(b) with no work.

mistakes.wrong: Writing the square root of a sum as the sum of the square roots.
mistakes.right: Roots do not distribute over addition; only the a + 2 root b split opens a nested root.

mistakes.wrong: Reading a to the power minus n as minus a to the n.
mistakes.right: A negative exponent flips the base: a to the power minus n is one over a to the n.

mistakes.wrong: Adding exponents when the bases differ.
mistakes.right: Convert to one prime base first; only same-base powers add exponents.

mistakes.wrong: Comparing surds of different orders by their radicands.
mistakes.right: Raise all surds to the LCM of the root orders and compare the integers.

mistakes.wrong: Splitting a + 2 root b without rewriting the middle term.
mistakes.right: Force the middle term into the 2 root b shape so b is the product, not the visible number.

subtopics.notes:
A power question always has the same escape route: write every number as a power of one prime. $1024$ is $2^{10}$ and also $4^5$; $81$ is $3^4$ and also $27^{4/3}$, because $27^4 = 81^3$. Once the bases match, only the exponents remain.

### The laws that move exponents
| Law | Statement |
|---|---|
| same base, product | $a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}$ |
| same base, quotient | $a^m \div a^n = a^{m-n}$ |
| power of a power | $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ |
| zero and negative | $a^0 = 1$, $a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^n}$ |
| fractional index | $a^{p/q} = \sqrt[q]{a^p}$ |

> **Rule:** Make every base the same prime first. Then add, subtract and multiply exponents; never touch the numbers again.

### Solving a power equation
$4^{x+1} \times 16^{2-x} = 64$ becomes $2^{2x+2} \times 2^{8-4x} = 2^6$, so $2x + 2 + 8 - 4x = 6$, giving $x = 2$. Fractional indices evaluate in the same spirit: $32^{2/5} = (2^5)^{2/5} = 2^2 = 4$, and $81^{3/4} = 27$.

### Rationalising with the conjugate
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate, the same terms with the flipped middle sign:
$$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a} \pm \sqrt{b}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{a} \mp \sqrt{b}}{a - b}$$
The product $(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b})(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b}) = a - b$ clears every root from the bottom.

### Telescoping chains
A sum like $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9}+\sqrt{8}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{8}+\sqrt{7}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{6}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}+\sqrt{5}}$ rationalises term by term into $\sqrt{9}-\sqrt{8} + \sqrt{8}-\sqrt{7} + \dots$, and the middle roots kill each other. Only the ends survive: $\sqrt{9} - \sqrt{5} = 3 - \sqrt{5}$.

> **Tip:** In a chain of $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{k}+\sqrt{k-1}}$ terms, write the answer as first root minus last root and skip the middle entirely.

### The a plus two root b split
To open $\sqrt{a + 2\sqrt{b}}$, hunt two numbers with sum $a$ and product $b$; the root is $\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y}$. For $\sqrt{7 + 4\sqrt{3}}$, write $4\sqrt{3}$ as $2\sqrt{12}$, so $x + y = 7$ and $xy = 12$: the pair is $4$ and $3$, giving $2 + \sqrt{3}$.

> **Watch:** $\sqrt{a+b}$ is not $\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}$. The split only works when the middle term is forced into the $2\sqrt{b}$ shape first.

### Comparing surds
Raise every surd to the LCM of the root orders, then compare plain integers. For $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt[3]{7}$, $\sqrt[4]{5}$, the orders 2, 3, 4 give LCM 12. Twelfth powers: $3^6 = 729$, $7^3 = 343$, $5^4 = 625$. So $\sqrt{3}$ is the largest.

### A surd and its reciprocal
If $x = a + \sqrt{b}$ and $a^2 - b = 1$, then $\dfrac{1}{x} = a - \sqrt{b}$. Check first: for $5 + 2\sqrt{6}$, $25 - 24 = 1$, so the reciprocal is $5 - 2\sqrt{6}$ and $x + \dfrac{1}{x} = 10$. If $a^2 - b$ is not a perfect square, do the long rationalisation instead.

patterns.name: Evaluate fractional and negative powers
patterns.howToSpot: Numbers raised to fractions or negatives, like $32^{2/5}$ or $81^{3/4}$, often mixed in one expression.
steps: Apply the fractional index: root first, then power.
Combine the results with ordinary arithmetic.
patterns.why: A fractional index is a root in disguise, and prime bases make the root visible.

patterns.name: Rationalisation and telescoping surd fractions
patterns.howToSpot: Fractions with roots in the denominator, or a long sum of such fractions with roots stepping down by one.
steps: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.
In a long sum, rationalise every term.
Watch the middle roots cancel in pairs.
Write the answer as first root minus last root.
patterns.why: Each term becomes a difference of roots that cancels with its neighbour, leaving only the two ends.

patterns.name: Root of a surd: the a plus two root b split
patterns.howToSpot: A square root wrapped around a number plus a root, like $\sqrt{9 + 4\sqrt{5}}$.
steps: Rewrite the middle term as $2\sqrt{b}$ if needed.
Find two numbers with sum $a$ and product $b$.
Answer is $\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y}$, or their difference when the middle sign is minus.
patterns.why: Squaring $\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y}$ returns exactly $x + y + 2\sqrt{xy}$.

patterns.name: Comparing surds of different orders
patterns.howToSpot: A list of roots with different orders, asking which is largest or smallest.
steps: Take the LCM of all the root orders.
Raise each surd to that LCM; roots disappear.
Compare the integers and read off the answer.
patterns.why: A common power turns every surd into an integer, and integers compare at a glance.

patterns.name: Solve an equation in powers
patterns.howToSpot: An unknown sits in the exponent, and the bases are powers of one number.
steps: Write every base as a power of the smallest prime present.
Collect the exponents of the left side into one.
Write the right side in the same base.
Equate exponents and solve the linear equation.
patterns.why: Equal bases make the exponent equation the only content left.

revision: One prime base; then exponents add, subtract or multiply.
Power of a power multiplies the exponents.
Conjugate rationalisation: flip the middle sign, divide by $a - b$.
Telescoping chain: answer is first root minus last root.
$\sqrt{a + 2\sqrt{b}} = \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y}$ with $x + y = a$, $xy = b$.
Compare surds at the LCM of the root orders.
$a^2 - b = 1$ makes the reciprocal $a - \sqrt{b}$.

subtopics.title: Square roots & cube roots
subtopics.concept: A square root question is answered by digit pairs and the unit-digit map; a cube root by digit triples and the swap map. Least-add and least-subtract questions sit between two neighbouring squares, and radicals are opened from the inside out.

tricks.title: Cube root by unit digit and leading group
tricks.body: The last digit of the cube gives the last digit of the root; the leading group, compared with the small cubes, gives the first digit.

steps: Groups: $175 \mid 616$, so the root has two digits.
Cube ends in $6$, and $6$ maps to itself: root $= 56$.

tricks.title: Square root by unit digit and size
tricks.body: Digit pairs fix the number of digits and the first digit; the last-digit map gives two candidates; one size check picks between them.

steps: Pairs $96 \mid 04$: two digits; $9^2 = 81 \le 96$, so it starts with $9$.
Ends in $4$, so the root ends in $2$ or $8$.

tricks.title: n equals k times k plus one radicals
tricks.body: Factor n into two consecutive integers. Plus signs give the larger one, minus signs the smaller.

mistakes.wrong: Miscounting decimal places in roots of decimals.
mistakes.right: Square root halves the decimal places; cube root divides them by three.

mistakes.wrong: Keeping the negative root when solving x squared equals a plus x.
mistakes.right: A radical expression is positive; take the positive root of the quadratic.

mistakes.wrong: Declaring a number a perfect square because it ends in 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.
mistakes.right: The unit digit only rules candidates out; confirm with digit pairing and a check.

mistakes.wrong: Swapping the add and subtract gaps.
mistakes.right: Subtract down to k squared; add up to the next square, k plus one squared.

mistakes.wrong: Opening a nested radical from the outermost root.
mistakes.right: Evaluate from the innermost root outward, one layer at a time.

subtopics.notes:
Every root question in this chapter is built on a perfect power, and the exam expects you to find it without long division. Two tools do it: the unit digit of the answer, and the size of the answer from digit grouping.

### The unit-digit maps
A perfect square ends only in $0, 1, 4, 5, 6$ or $9$; the digits $2, 3, 7, 8$ never appear. The map from root to square is short: root ending $1$ or $9$ gives square ending $1$. Root ending $2$ or $8$ gives $4$, and $3$ or $7$ gives $9$. Root ending $4$ or $6$ gives $6$, and $5$ gives $5$.
Cube digits are even friendlier: $1, 4, 5, 6, 9, 0$ map to themselves, and $2$ swaps with $8$, $3$ with $7$.

> **Rule:** For a cube root, the last digit of the cube gives the last digit of the root directly, using the swap pairs 2 with 8 and 3 with 7.

### Size from digit grouping
Pair the digits of a square from the right: the number of pairs equals the digits in the root. Group a cube in threes the same way. For $\sqrt{9604}$: pairs $96 \mid 04$, so a two-digit root; $9^2 = 81 \le 96$, so it starts with $9$. Ending $4$ means root ends in $2$ or $8$; since $95^2 = 9025$ is too small, the root is $98$.
For a cube root, the leading group fixes the first digit: the largest cube not exceeding it. In $\sqrt[3]{175616}$, groups are $175 \mid 616$; $5^3 = 125 \le 175 < 216 = 6^3$, so the root starts with $5$ and ends with $6$: answer $56$.

### Roots of decimals
Count decimal places. A square root halves them: $0.0169$ has four places, so its root has two: $0.13$. A cube root divides them by three: $0.000064$ has six places, root $0.04$. Combine both: $\sqrt{1.69} + \sqrt{0.0169} = 1.3 + 0.13 = 1.43$.

> **Watch:** A unit digit can only rule a perfect square out, never confirm it. Always finish with the size check.

### Least number to add or subtract
Bracket $N$ between neighbouring squares $k^2$ and $(k+1)^2$.
- Subtract case: answer is $N - k^2$, the gap down.
- Add case: answer is $(k+1)^2 - N$, the gap up.
For $456$: $21^2 = 441$ and $22^2 = 484$, so subtracting $456 - 441 = 15$ lands on $441$. For $2000$: $44^2 = 1936$ and $45^2 = 2025$, so adding $2025 - 2000 = 25$ lands on $2025$.

### Nested radicals: inside out
Replace the deepest root first; each layer then becomes a perfect square. $\sqrt{20 + \sqrt{19 + \sqrt{36}}}$: innermost $\sqrt{36} = 6$; then $\sqrt{19 + 6} = \sqrt{25} = 5$; then $\sqrt{20 + 5} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.

> **Tip:** Setters place each layer to collapse exactly. If a layer does not land on a perfect square, recheck the inner layer before forcing on.

### Infinite radicals
Call the whole expression $x$; the tail equals $x$ again, so $x = \sqrt{a + x}$. Then $x^2 - x - a = 0$; keep the positive root. Fast path: if $a = k(k+1)$, the answer is $k + 1$. Check with $12 = 3 \times 4$: $4^2 = 12 + 4$ holds, so $\sqrt{12 + \sqrt{12 + \cdots}} = 4$. The product form $\sqrt{x\sqrt{x\sqrt{x \cdots}}}$ equals $x$ itself.

### Root equations with an unknown
Isolate the root on one side and square once. $\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{x}{225}} = \dfrac{16}{15}$ gives $1 + \dfrac{x}{225} = \dfrac{256}{225}$, so $x = 31$. Square both sides only after the root stands alone.

patterns.name: Square root or cube root of a perfect power
patterns.howToSpot: A clean big number sits under a root sign and the options are whole numbers.
patterns.formula: \text{digit pairs (squares) or triples (cubes) plus the unit-digit map}
steps: Group digits from the right: pairs for a square root, triples for a cube root.
Read the size from the leading group.
Read the last digit from the map or swap map.
Verify by squaring or cubing the candidate.
patterns.why: The grouping gives size, the unit digit gives the tail; together they pin the answer without long division.

steps: Ending $6$ maps to itself: root $56$; check $56^3 = 175616$.

patterns.name: Least number to add or subtract to reach a perfect square
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the least number added to or subtracted from N so the result is a perfect square.
steps: Find $k$, the whole part of the square root of $N$.
Subtract case: answer $N - k^2$; add case: answer $(k+1)^2 - N$.
patterns.why: The nearest squares on the two sides of $N$ are exactly $k^2$ and $(k+1)^2$.

example.q: Find the least number that must be added to $2000$ to make it a perfect square.

patterns.name: Nested radicals, worked from the inside
patterns.howToSpot: A finite stack of square roots, each wrapped around the previous result.
steps: Replace the deepest root with its value.
Add or combine outward one layer at a time.
Each layer should land on a perfect square.
patterns.why: Only the innermost layer is a number you can root immediately; every outer layer waits for it.

patterns.name: Infinite radicals
patterns.howToSpot: The same pattern repeats forever, shown by dots; the word infinite may appear.
steps: Spot the tail equals $x$ again and build the equation.
Solve and keep the positive root.
Fast path: factor $a$ as $k(k+1)$; the answer is $k + 1$.
patterns.why: Self-similarity turns the endless tower into one short quadratic.

patterns.name: Roots of decimals
patterns.howToSpot: A decimal sits under the root sign, like $1.69$ or $0.000064$.
patterns.formula: \text{decimal places halve (square root) or divide by three (cube root)}
steps: Count the decimal places of the number.
Halve them for a square root; take a third for a cube root.
Root the digits as a whole number and place the point.
patterns.why: Rooting affects the place values exactly as the index divides the decimal count.

revision: Perfect squares end in $0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9$; cubes use the swap map $2 \leftrightarrow 8$, $3 \leftrightarrow 7$.
Digit pairs size a square root; digit triples size a cube root.
Subtract $N - k^2$; add $(k+1)^2 - N$.
Nested radicals open from the inside out.
$x = \sqrt{a + x}$; if $a = k(k+1)$, the answer is $k + 1$.
Product form $\sqrt{x\sqrt{x\cdots}}$ equals $x$.

subtopics.title: Approximation
subtopics.concept: An approximation question hands you ugly numbers on purpose and options that sit far apart. Round every number to a friendly value, compute exactly on the rounded numbers, and pick the nearest option.

formulas.name: Percentage swap
formulas.tex: x\% \text{ of } y = y\% \text{ of } x

tricks.title: Swap the percentage
tricks.body: x percent of y equals y percent of x. Flip to whichever side has the nicer multiplier.

tricks.title: Balanced rounding for products
tricks.body: Round one factor up and the other down. The two errors cancel and the product stays close.

tricks.title: Anchors before bases
tricks.body: Turn the percent into its fraction anchor first, then apply it to the rounded base.

mistakes.wrong: Rounding every number in a product in the same direction.
mistakes.right: Round one factor up and the other down so errors cancel.

mistakes.wrong: Computing the exact value with long multiplication.
mistakes.right: Round, compute on friendly numbers, pick the nearest option; the spacing allows it.

mistakes.wrong: Treating (?)% as a number and of ? as a percentage.
mistakes.right: The percent sign on the question mark makes the unknown a percent; otherwise it is a plain number.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting BODMAS order while approximating.
mistakes.right: The 'of' product still outranks the division sign in rounded work too.

subtopics.notes:
When a question starts with 'what approximate value', it is permission to round. The numbers are deliberately awkward, like $399.87$ or $24.98\%$, and the options sit $5$ to $10$ percent apart. Rounding error stays near one percent, so the nearest option is safe.

### The rounding rules
Round decimals to the nearest whole number: $49.98$ to $50$, $15.02$ to $15$, $23.9$ to $24$. Snap roots and powers to neighbours: $\sqrt{1224.9}$ sits next to $35^2 = 1225$, and $(29.98)^2$ is $30^2 = 900$ for all practical purposes.

> **Rule:** Round first, then compute exactly on the rounded numbers. Never carry ugly decimals through five steps.

### Percentage anchors, learned cold
| Fraction | Percent | Fraction | Percent |
|---|---|---|---|
| $1/2$ | $50\%$ | $1/8$ | $12.5\%$ |
| $1/3$ | $33.3\%$ | $1/9$ | $11.1\%$ |
| $1/4$ | $25\%$ | $1/12$ | $8.3\%$ |
| $1/5$ | $20\%$ | $3/8$ | $37.5\%$ |
| $1/6$ | $16.7\%$ | $2/3$ | $66.7\%$ |

So $16.98\%$ of $600$ reads as one sixth of $600$, about $100$. Percentage times round bases is a one-step mental product.

> **Tip:** Convert the percent to its fraction anchor before touching the base number; $37.5\%$ of $480$ is three eighths of $480$, which is $180$.

### Balanced rounding in products
When two rounded numbers multiply, round one up and the other down so the errors cancel. $15.02 \times 23.9$ becomes $15 \times 24 = 360$, not $15 \times 24$ after rounding both up. One factor down, one factor up, every time.

### Roots and powers near perfect values
Setters place roots beside perfect powers on purpose. $\sqrt{3968.9}$ is $63$ because $63^2 = 3969$; $\sqrt[3]{29791.03}$ is $31$ because $31^3 = 29791$. Spot the neighbour first, then read the root off it.

### Size and direction checks
Decide the size region before computing: tens, hundreds or thousands. One decoy option usually lives in each region. For unknowns, direction matters: $18\%$ of $?$ equals $117$ means $? = 117$ divided by $0.18$, a bigger number; $(?)\%$ of $800$ equals $240$ means $?$ is itself a percentage, here $30$.

> **Watch:** A question mark before the percent sign asks for a percent; a question mark after 'of' asks for a number. Mixing them flips the answer by a factor of ten.

### One clean run
$19.98\%$ of $200 + 11.99 \times 6$: one fifth of $200$ is $40$, and $12 \times 6 = 72$, so about $112$. Round, compute once, choose, move on.

> **Remember:** An approximation question is a reading test, not an arithmetic test. The setter wrote ugly numbers so that rounding is the intended path; the student who multiplies $399.87$ by hand has already lost the time race.

patterns.name: Mixed chain with percent, multiply and divide
patterns.howToSpot: A question mark with 'approximately equals' and a chain mixing % of, products and divisions of decimals.
steps: Round each decimal to its nearest friendly value.
Replace the percent with its fraction anchor.
Compute the chain with BODMAS order.
Pick the option nearest to the result.
patterns.why: Options sit several percent apart while rounding error stays near one percent.

patterns.name: Percentage chains and unknown percent equations
patterns.howToSpot: Two percent terms combined, or an equation where the unknown is itself a percentage.
steps: Round the base and the targets.
Shift the known numbers to the far side first.
Divide the remainder by the base and scale by 100.
patterns.why: After shifting, the equation is one division on rounded numbers.

patterns.name: Roots and powers inside an approximation
patterns.howToSpot: Near-perfect squares and cubes hide inside the expression, like $(29.98)^2$ or $\sqrt{1224.9}$.
steps: Snap each square to the rounded base squared.
Snap each root to the neighbouring perfect power.
patterns.why: Setters build these expressions within a whisker of perfect powers, so snapping loses almost nothing.

patterns.name: Find the missing value
patterns.howToSpot: The question mark is a whole term of the equation, not necessarily a percentage.
steps: Evaluate every term that holds no question mark.
Move it across the equals sign with the inverse operation.
Round the result and sanity-check its size.
patterns.why: It is one move of algebra applied to rounded numbers.

patterns.name: Round before dividing
patterns.howToSpot: An awkward division like $399.87 \div 7.99$, often mixed with other rounded terms.
patterns.formula: \text{round divisor and dividend to compatible values}
steps: Round the divisor to a friendly one-digit number.
Round the dividend so the division comes out clean.
Finish the remaining terms and combine.
patterns.why: A clean quotient beats a correct-but-slow long division, because options are far apart.

revision: Round every number first; compute exactly on rounded values.
Percent to fraction anchor before touching the base.
Products: round one factor up, one down.
Roots sit beside perfect powers; read the neighbour.
Check size region and the direction of the unknown percent.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A long mixed expression with ÷, ×, 'of', brackets and a vinculum. The word 'of' is the trap marker.
pyqPatterns.approach: Follow VBODMAS strictly: vinculum, brackets innermost first, then 'of' (it multiplies but comes before ÷ and ×), then ÷ and × left to right, then + and −. A minus before a bracket flips every sign inside.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A fraction whose top is a sum/difference of cubes (often decimals) and whose bottom is a²∓ab+b² or a²±ab+b².
pyqPatterns.approach: Match the denominator to the identity factor and cancel: (a³+b³)/(a²−ab+b²) = a+b; (a³−b³)/(a²+ab+b²) = a−b. Read the middle sign carefully — minus below pairs with plus above.
Square the given: $x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2} = k^2 - 2$ (plus) or $k^2 + 2$ (minus). Cube: $k^3 \mp 3k$. Fourth power: square the squared result and subtract 2.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Indices equation with a common base
pyqPatterns.approach: Write every term as a power of one prime (4 = 2², 25 = 5²). Take the common power outside if it is a sum. Then equate the exponents.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Fractions like $\frac{1}{\sqrt7-\sqrt6}$, sums of conjugate fractions, or a surd plus its reciprocal.
pyqPatterns.approach: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate. Telescoping chains collapse to (first root − last root). If x = a+2√b type, then 1/x is the conjugate a−2√b.

example.solution: Each term is $\sqrt k - \sqrt{k-1}$; the sum collapses to $3 - 1 = 2$.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Expressions like $\sqrt{11+6\sqrt2}$ or $\sqrt{7+4\sqrt3}$ (and the two-root sum/difference versions).
pyqPatterns.approach: Rewrite as $\sqrt{a+2\sqrt b}$; split $a = x+y$ with $xy = b$; the value is $\sqrt x+\sqrt y$. For a pair like $\sqrt{7+4\sqrt3} \pm \sqrt{7-4\sqrt3}$, take $x = 2+\sqrt3$, $y = 2-\sqrt3$ and add or subtract.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Cube and square roots of perfect powers; least number for a square
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find ∛9261', '√11025', or 'least number to add/subtract to N to make a perfect square'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cube root: group digits in threes, use the unit-digit swap map (2↔8, 3↔7) plus a size check. Square root: digit pairs, last-digit map and neighbours. For least add/subtract, bracket N between k² and (k+1)².

example.q: Least number to add to 1300 for a perfect square?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: $\sqrt{6+\sqrt{6+\dots}}$, $\sqrt{20\times\sqrt{20\times\dots}}$, or a finite nest like $\sqrt{30+\sqrt{24+\sqrt{144}}}$. (already exists as solved example — same type, new numbers)
pyqPatterns.approach: Infinite plus-radical: solve $x^2 = a + x$ (or use $a = k(k+1)$ → answer $k+1$). Infinite product-radical: the answer is $a$. Finite nests: work from the innermost root outward.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Approximation with percentages, products and roots
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'What approximate value comes in place of ?' with decimals like 1199.8, 24.98%, √2303.9.
pyqPatterns.approach: Round every number to a friendly value (nearest ten, percentage → fraction, root → nearest perfect power), compute mentally, and pick the closest option. Options are spaced far apart; do not chase exact decimals.

solvedExamples.shortcut: Each level is 1 + (reciprocal of the level below): 3/2 → 5/3 → 8/5 (Fibonacci ratios: 2/1, 3/2, 5/3, 8/5).

solvedExamples.solution:
$7 + 4\sqrt{3} = 7 + 2\sqrt{12}$: two numbers with sum 7 and product 12 are 4 and 3.
So $\sqrt{7 + 4\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{4} + \sqrt{3} = 2 + \sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{7 - 4\sqrt{3}} = 2 - \sqrt{3}$.
Sum $= (2 + \sqrt{3}) + (2 - \sqrt{3}) = 4$.

solvedExamples.q: What is the least number that must be subtracted from 7250 to make it a perfect square?
solvedExamples.solution:
$85^2 = 7225$ and $86^2 = 7396$. The largest perfect square $\le 7250$ is 7225.
Number to subtract = 7250 − 7225 = **25**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 7250 ≈ 85² (since 85² = 7225, easy from '5-ending' squares: 8 × 9 = 72 → 7225). Difference 25. (146 is the amount to ADD to reach 86² — a common trap.)

solvedExamples.solution:
Let $a = 0.73$, $b = 0.27$. The expression is $\frac{a^3 + b^3}{a^2 - ab + b^2}$.
Since $a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)$, the value is $a + b = 0.73 + 0.27 = 1$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Cubes on top, 'minus middle term' below ⇒ answer = a + b = 1.

practice.shortcut: Treat '4 of 3' as a bracket (12). Trap: ignoring 'of' gives 48 ÷ 4 × 3 = 36 and the answer 37.
169 → 13, 144 → 12, 13 × 12 = 156. Decimal places: 4 + 2 = 6 inside the root → 3 outside ⇒ 0.156.
Cube root of 27 is 3, squared 9. Fourth root of 16 is 2, cubed 8, negative index → 1/8. Answer 9/8.

4913 ends in 3 ⇒ the cube root ends in 7 (since $7^3 = 343$).
Leading group (digits before the last three) = 4: $1^3 = 1 \le 4 < 8 = 2^3$ ⇒ tens digit 1.
Root $= 17$. Check: $17^3 = 4913$ ✓.

Work strictly inside-out: 1 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 3.

practice.q: Which of the following is the largest? $\sqrt[3]{4},\ \sqrt{2},\ \sqrt[6]{10},\ \sqrt[4]{5}$
practice.shortcut: Quick decimals: $\sqrt[3]{4} \approx 1.59$, $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$, $\sqrt[6]{10} \approx 1.47$, $\sqrt[4]{5} \approx 1.50$.
Take out the smaller power: bracket = 10, so $3^x = 81$ ⇒ $x = 4$.

practice.q: What approximate value should come in place of '?': $29.97\% \text{ of } 1199.8 + 15.02 \times 23.99 = \ ?$
If $x = 3 + 2\sqrt{2}$, then the value of $\sqrt{x} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ is:
practice.shortcut:
$\left(\sqrt{x} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^2 = x + \frac{1}{x} - 2$.
$\frac{1}{x} = 3 - 2\sqrt{2}$ (since $9 - 8 = 1$) ⇒ $x + \frac{1}{x} = 6$ ⇒ square $= 4$ ⇒ value $= 2$.
Rule: when the bases multiply ($2 \times 3 = 6$), the reciprocals of the exponents add. Check with numbers: $2^{\log_2 36} = 3^{\log_3 36} = 6^2$ gives $c = 2$ and $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ matches.
Every denominator number is exactly double the numerator one (0.2 = 2 × 0.1, 0.04 = 2 × 0.02), so denominator $= 2^3 \times$ numerator ⇒ answer $= \frac{1}{8} = 0.125$.
Trap 38 comes from reading 'of' as plain ×: $(64 \div 4) \times 2 = 32$, then $32 + 24 - 18 = 38$.
Trap 18: reading 'of' as plain × gives $24 \div 4 \times 3 = 18$, and $36 - 18 = 18$.

practice.q: What value in place of '?': $48 \div ? \text{ of } 3 + 4 = 8$
practice.shortcut: Check: $48 \div 4 \text{ of } 3 = 48 \div 12 = 4$, and $4 + 4 = 8$ ✓.
Minus before $[6 - 8]$ changes it to $+2$.
The whole $1 + \frac{1}{\dots}$ block sits under the first division.

practice.q: If $x = 34$ and $y = 16$, find the value of $(x+y)^2 + (x-y)^2$.
practice.shortcut: Trap 1412 is $x^2 + y^2$ — you forgot the factor 2.
Minus version: add 2, not subtract.

practice.q: If $a + b = 10$ and $ab = 21$, find the value of $a^2 + b^2$.
If $a + b = 7$ and $ab = 12$, find the value of $a^3 + b^3$.
practice.shortcut: Check: the numbers are 3 and 4, and $27 + 64 = 91$ ✓.

$25 - 17 - 8 = 0$, so the cubes add up to $3abc$:
$3 \times 25 \times (-17) \times (-8) = 3 \times 25 \times 136 = 10200$.

practice.q: If $2^{x+3} \times 4^{x-1} = 128$, what is the value of $x$?

practice.solution: Multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt7 + \sqrt6$: denominator $= 7 - 6 = 1$. Value $= \sqrt7 + \sqrt6$.

Rationalise each term with its conjugate: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}+\sqrt{k-1}} = \sqrt{k} - \sqrt{k-1}$.
The sum collapses (telescopes): $(\sqrt9 - \sqrt8) + (\sqrt8 - \sqrt7) + \dots + (\sqrt2 - 1) = \sqrt9 - 1 = 2$.
practice.shortcut: Every middle surd appears twice with opposite signs and cancels.

practice.q: Which of the following is the largest? $\sqrt{3},\ \sqrt[4]{7},\ \sqrt[3]{5},\ \sqrt[6]{25}$
practice.solution:
Raise each to the power 12 (LCM of 2, 3, 4, 6):
$\sqrt3 \to 3^6 = 729$; $\sqrt[4]{7} \to 7^3 = 343$; $\sqrt[3]{5} \to 5^4 = 625$; $\sqrt[6]{25} \to 25^2 = 625$.
Largest base value 729 → $\sqrt3$ is the largest.
practice.shortcut: The 6th root of 25 equals 5 to the 1/3 — it ties with ∛5.

practice.q: Which of the two numbers is greater: $\sqrt[3]{4}$ or $\sqrt[4]{6}$?

practice.solution:
Digit pairs from the right: 1 | 10 | 25 → a three-digit root.
$100^2 = 10000$ and $110^2 = 12100$, so the root is between 100 and 110. A square ending in 25 comes from a root ending in 5 → **105**.
Check: $105^2 = 11025$ ✓.

Groups of three from the right: 9 | 261 → a two-digit root.
Cube ends in 1 → root ends in 1 (or 9 wait: only 1³ ends in 1). First group $8 \le 9$ → tens digit 2. Root = **21**.
practice.shortcut: Unit-digit map: cube ends 1 → root ends 1; 2³ = 8 fits under 9.
6 decimal places → 2 decimal places in the root.

practice.q: If $\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{x}{225}} = \dfrac{16}{15}$, what is the value of $x$?

practice.solution:
Let $x = \sqrt{6 + \sqrt{6 + \dots}}$. Then $x^2 = 6 + x$, i.e. $x^2 - x - 6 = 0$.
$(x-3)(x+2) = 0$ → $x = 3$ (positive root).
practice.shortcut: Shortcut: 6 = 2 × 3 = k(k+1) with k = 2 → answer k + 1 = 3.

practice.solution:
Let $x = \sqrt{20x}$. Squaring: $x^2 = 20x$ → $x = 20$ (non-zero root).
The infinite product-radical always equals the number itself.

practice.q: What approximate value will come in place of '?': $29.9\% \text{ of } 1199.8 + 15.02 \times 23.9 = \ ?$
practice.solution:
Round: $30\%$ of $1200 = 360$; $15 \times 24 = 360$.
Answer $≈ 360 + 360 = 720$. (Exact value $717.7$. Options are spaced ~10% apart, so rounding is safe.)
